case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a free sports-news website that publishes short video clips qualifies as a “video tape service provider” under the Video Privacy Protection Act such that it can be liable for disclosing users’ video-viewing information.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 2710 (the Video Privacy Protection Act of 1988), including the definitions and disclosure prohibition in § 2710(a) and § 2710(b)(1).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Salazar argues the Sixth Circuit adopted an overly narrow interpretation of the VPPA that effectively limits the statute to legacy video-rental businesses, contrary to the text and purpose of protecting consumers’ privacy in video-viewing choices. He contends the Court should resolve a circuit split over the meaning of “video tape service provider,” and emphasizes that this case is a clean vehicle because it comes on final judgment and does not present the interlocutory/serial-pleading complications present in the related NBA v. Salazar petition.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Paramount/247Sports argues certiorari should be denied because the VPPA was aimed at businesses like video rental/sales (e.g., video cassette rental records) and does not naturally extend to a free, ad-supported sports-news site with articles, photos, and short video clips. Respondent also contends the petition is a poor vehicle because, even if the Court resolved the “consumer/video service provider” question, Salazar’s complaint would still fail on other independent grounds (including disputes about what counts as “personally identifiable information” and/or standing), and the Court should allow further percolation rather than decide the issue in a case with multiple potentially dispositive defects.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that reading “delivery” to exclude internet video risks hollowing out the VPPA’s privacy purpose—deserves respect, but under my minimalist approach we should avoid a broad, technology-updating construction when narrower grounds may resolve the case. Justice Kagan’s warning that an expansive reading would collapse the limiting phrase “engaged in the business” reinforces the institutional risk of issuing an unnecessary statutory-scope ruling here. In addition, the standing and PII defects I flagged remain serious after TransUnion; even if some lower courts (as Sotomayor notes via Perry/Eichenberger) have found standing in VPPA cases, this record may not present a clean, traditionally analogous concrete harm, making this a poor vehicle for a sweeping merits pronouncement. I would therefore affirm for Respondent on narrower, case-dispositive grounds without definitively resolving the full “video tape service provider” question.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Congress used functional language—“delivery” of “similar audio visual materials”—capable of applying to new technologies, and that many modern users are “subscribers.” But under the original public meaning in 1988, § 2710(a)(4) is anchored by the enumerated model (“prerecorded video cassette tapes”) and the business qualifier (“engaged in the business”), and the associated-words canons that Justice Gorsuch and Justice Alito invoke (as in Yates) prevent “similar” from becoming a technology-updating license that erases those limits. The statutory structure tying “consumer” to a renter/purchaser/subscriber relationship with “such provider” still presupposes a video-distribution enterprise, not ordinary web browsing on a general-interest sports site where clips are incidental. Chief Justice Roberts’s TransUnion/vehicle concerns reinforce caution, but even setting standing and PII aside, Sotomayor’s purposive approach cannot overcome the enacted text as originally understood.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that “delivery” and the statute’s privacy purpose should be read functionally to cover modern streaming—cannot overcome the VPPA’s enacted limiting language. The phrase “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” read with the linked definition of “consumer” as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber” of “such provider,” is transaction- and provider-specific; it does not naturally extend to a general sports-news site where video clips are ancillary, even if users create accounts. Justice Roberts’s vehicle concerns (PII and TransUnion standing) further counsel against issuing any broad, technology-updating construction here, but even on the merits the associated-words canons Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch invoke (as in Yates) keep “similar audio visual materials” tethered to the cassette-tape model rather than transforming the VPPA into a general internet-tracking statute.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s vehicle caution seriously, but I do not see it as a reason to construe “video tape service provider” artificially narrowly; standing/PII can be addressed directly on their own terms without hollowing out the statute’s operative coverage in the internet era. Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch are right that “engaged in the business” must do limiting work, yet that limitation can be satisfied where an entity systematically offers video programming to users (often through accounts or subscriptions) as a meaningful line of business, even if it also provides text content—otherwise we freeze “delivery” and “similar audio visual materials” to 1988 distribution forms despite Congress’s functional phrasing. Justice Thomas’s emphasis on the “consumer” definition is narrowing, but “subscriber” plausibly maps onto modern subscription/account relationships, and it would be perverse to treat pervasive, involuntary tracking of viewing choices as beyond the VPPA’s core concern simply because technology changed. Precedents like Yates (invoked by several colleagues) caution against untethered expansion, but they do not require reading “similar audio visual materials” so crabbed that it defeats Congress’s central privacy protection for vulnerable users in today’s video ecosystem.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that “delivery” and “similar audio visual materials” can be read in a technologically adaptable way so the VPPA’s privacy purpose is not frozen in 1988. But under my pragmatic textualism, that updating impulse cannot nullify the statute’s narrowing words—especially “engaged in the business” and the transaction-linked definition of “consumer” as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber”—which, as Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch stress, signal a class of entities whose business is providing video media, not general news sites where clips are ancillary. I also find Chief Justice Roberts’s vehicle concern persuasive: if standing/PII issues (in the shadow of TransUnion) could dispose of the case, it is institutionally imprudent to announce a broad, technology-updating construction that risks turning the VPPA into a general internet-tracking statute. Yates-style contextual limits, invoked by several colleagues, reinforces that “similar” must do real work rather than becoming an all-purpose catchall.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that “delivery” can be a functional term and that the VPPA’s privacy purpose is weighty, but under a textualist/originalist reading we must give effect to Congress’s limiting language: a “video tape service provider” is one “engaged in the business” of “rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” which—under noscitur a sociis/ejusdem generis as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett stress—confines “similar” to media akin to the enumerated cassette-tape model rather than any website with incidental clips. Her point that modern users can be “subscribers” does not solve the structural problem: § 2710(a)(1)’s “renter, purchaser, or subscriber” ties consumption to a provider-centric, transactional relationship, not ordinary web browsing. Chief Justice Roberts’s vehicle concerns (PII and TransUnion standing) further reinforce that we should not use this case to update the statute beyond its enacted bounds, especially where alternative grounds may dispose of it. Sotomayor’s privacy-analogy argument is compelling as policy, but it does not overcome the statute’s text and context as publicly understood in 1988.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that “delivery … of similar audio visual materials” should be read functionally so the VPPA’s privacy protection remains effective in the internet era, but under my institutionalist, precedent- and text-respecting approach the limiting phrase “engaged in the business” and the linked definition of “consumer” as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber” still tether the statute to provider-centric, transactional relationships rather than incidental web browsing. Justice Thomas’s contextual reading—reinforced by Yates’s associated-words logic—persuasively shows that “similar audio visual materials” cannot be allowed to swallow the cassette-tape-centered frame Congress enacted without effectively rewriting the statute. Chief Justice Roberts’s vehicle concern also matters here: if PII or Article III injury under TransUnion can independently dispose of the case, we should avoid an unnecessary, sweeping pronouncement about nationwide VPPA coverage that could destabilize doctrine and the Court’s legitimacy. Sotomayor’s point that many sites have “subscribers” narrows the gap, but it still does not overcome the statute’s focus on entities whose business is providing audiovisual materials, not general-interest sites where clips are ancillary.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that the VPPA’s privacy-protective purpose should not be frozen in 1988 technology and that “delivery” could naturally extend to streaming/web video. But under a textualist approach, the phrase “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials” must be read as a unit, and the associated-words canons (as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas emphasize, consistent with Yates) counsel that “similar audio visual materials” is confined to materials akin to the enumerated prerecorded media rather than any website incidentally hosting clips. The statute’s structure—particularly the “consumer” definition keyed to a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber” of “such provider”—supports Justice Kagan’s point that Congress targeted a specific class of video-provision transactions, not general web browsing. Finally, Chief Justice Roberts’ vehicle concern reinforces my view that we should avoid a broad merits pronouncement where PII and TransUnion standing may independently resolve the case, making respondent the sound disposition here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that the VPPA’s privacy purpose would be hollowed out if “delivery” cannot reach modern web video—presses on a real practical consequence, and her analogy to historically cognizable privacy harms under TransUnion is not frivolous. But even crediting the statute’s remedial aim, I agree with Justice Kagan that the limiting phrase “engaged in the business” must do work; treating a general-interest news site with incidental clips as a “video tape service provider” risks collapsing the narrowing terms and turning VPPA into a broad internet-tracking regime Congress did not clearly enact. Chief Justice Roberts’s vehicle concerns also matter under my pragmatic approach: if PII or Article III injury is independently dispositive, it is institutionally and procedurally unsound to issue a sweeping merits construction here. I therefore remain with Respondent because Sotomayor’s purpose-based reading does not, in my view, overcome the statute’s structure tying “consumers” to renter/purchaser/subscriber relationships with a provider whose business is video distribution in a more direct sense.

John Roberts.reasoning: I would vote for Respondent on narrow, vehicle-based grounds: even if we clarified the scope of “video tape service provider” in 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a), this case appears to present other potentially dispositive issues—particularly whether the alleged disclosure constitutes “personally identifiable information” under § 2710(a)(3) and whether Article III injury is adequately pleaded after TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez. Deciding the definitional question in a case with multiple independent defects risks an advisory ruling and threatens institutional legitimacy, especially where lower courts (e.g., Eichenberger v. ESPN and Perry v. CNN) have been resolving VPPA online cases on alternative grounds and further percolation is ongoing. Consistent with our preference for narrow resolution and avoidance of unnecessary statutory pronouncements, I would not extend (or limit) the VPPA’s provider definition here absent a clean posture requiring that decision.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The VPPA defines a “video tape service provider” as one “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), and that text—read in its ordinary 1988 public meaning—targets businesses whose business is providing video media akin to prerecorded cassettes, not a mixed-content, free sports-news website that incidentally hosts short clips. The pairing of definitions confirms the narrow scope: a “consumer” is a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber,” § 2710(a)(1), of “such provider,” § 2710(b)(1), which aligns with rental/sale/subscription-based delivery of audiovisual materials rather than general web browsing. “Similar” must do limiting work, and we should not transform an anti–video-store-disclosure statute into a general internet-tracking regime absent clear textual authorization. Consistent with the textual limiting approach in Yates v. United States, 574 U.S. 528 (2015), the statute should not be stretched beyond the kind of business Congress described.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The VPPA defines a “video tape service provider” as a person “engaged in the business . . . of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), and that language—read in context—targets entities whose business is providing video materials, not a general sports-news website that incidentally embeds short clips. Applying the associated-words canons (noscitur a sociis/ejusdem generis), “similar audio visual materials” should be limited by its association with “rental” and “sale” of “prerecorded video cassette tapes,” rather than expanded to cover any modern website hosting videos, as in Yates v. United States, 574 U.S. 528, 543–44 (2015). Extending the statute to free, ad-supported news sites would broaden an older statute beyond its practical and textual limits, creating sweeping privacy liability for ordinary web publishers without a clear congressional directive. Given those textual constraints, and the respondent’s additional vehicle concerns (including PII/standing issues under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021)), certiorari should be denied and the judgment below upheld.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The VPPA’s text covers any “video tape service provider” engaged in “rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), and a modern sports site that delivers short video clips to users plausibly fits that functional description rather than being limited to legacy brick-and-mortar rental stores. The statute’s core purpose is to prevent disclosure of individuals’ video-viewing choices, § 2710(b)(1), a privacy interest that is especially salient for ordinary users who cannot realistically bargain over tracking practices; narrowing coverage to “video stores” would undercut that protection in today’s streaming/web ecosystem. Consistent with Perry v. Cable News Network, Inc. and Eichenberger v. ESPN, Inc., the harm Congress targeted is an invasion of privacy akin to traditional intrusion upon seclusion, supporting a pragmatic reading that gives the statute ongoing force rather than a technology-bound one. Although respondent raises vehicle concerns (PII/standing), multiple circuits have recognized standing for VPPA disclosure claims (e.g., In re Nickelodeon; Perry; Eichenberger), and the statutory-coverage question is sufficiently important and recurring to warrant review and correction of an unduly cramped interpretation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2710(a)(4) defines a “video tape service provider” as a person “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” and that phrasing most naturally points to entities whose business is video distribution, not a general-interest sports-news site where short clips are ancillary to articles and photos. Reading “delivery” and “similar audio visual materials” to sweep in any website that embeds clips risks collapsing the limiting words “engaged in the business” and producing an unworkable, overbroad regime that Congress did not clearly enact. While the VPPA’s privacy purpose is real, the better pragmatic-textual middle ground is to leave major expansion of the statute to Congress and allow further percolation in other cases, especially given respondent’s vehicle objections (independent issues like PII/standing). Yates v. United States and Fischer v. United States counsel against interpretations that disregard textual limits in the name of broad statutory purpose.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The VPPA defines a “video tape service provider” as one engaged in the “rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), and the linked definition of “consumer” confirms the statute targets that particular class of transactions, § 2710(a)(1). Reading “similar audio visual materials” in context using noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis, the statute most naturally covers materials like the enumerated “prerecorded video cassette tapes,” not a general-interest, free, ad-supported sports-news site that merely includes short clips; stretching the term to any website with videos would effectively erase the limiting words Congress chose. As in Yates v. United States, 574 U.S. 528 (2015), we should resist interpretations that turn a statute aimed at a specific category into an all-purpose mandate untethered from its text and surrounding terms. Where Congress has not spoken clearly to extend this 1988 statute to today’s ubiquitous web-video ecosystem, separation-of-powers principles counsel leaving that policy judgment to the legislature, not the courts.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The VPPA’s definition of “video tape service provider” must be read in statutory context, and the phrase “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), points to businesses whose commercial function is providing audiovisual works—not a general-interest, free sports-news site that incidentally hosts short clips. Applying the associated-words canon, we should avoid reading general terms so broadly that they become inconsistent with accompanying, more specific words; Yates v. United States supports cabining “delivery” and related terms to the kind of audiovisual-goods-and-services enterprises Congress had in mind in 1988. History and practical workability also counsel restraint in extending an older privacy statute to modern, ad-supported websites absent clearer congressional direction, particularly where respondent argues the case may be a poor vehicle due to other independent defects (e.g., PII/standing issues under Spokeo and TransUnion). Accordingly, I would vote for respondent on the ground that the website is not a covered “video tape service provider” under § 2710.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The VPPA’s definition of “video tape service provider” covers a person “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4), and the best textual reading—guided by noscitur a sociis/ejusdem generis—treats “similar audio visual materials” as limited by the specific, commercially distributed prerecorded “video cassette tapes” listed alongside it. Under Yates v. United States, 574 U.S. 528, 543–44 (2015), we avoid giving a general phrase a breadth inconsistent with its accompanying words, and a free, ad-supported sports-news site offering short clips as ancillary content does not naturally fit a business of renting, selling, or delivering prerecorded video materials in the sense Congress used in 1988. While some circuits have read the VPPA more broadly for streaming/video apps, this petition also presents serious vehicle concerns because other independent issues (e.g., whether the alleged disclosure is “personally identifiable information” and whether plaintiff has a concrete injury) can be dispositive under Spokeo, 578 U.S. 330 (2016), and TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021). In light of the statute’s text and the risk of deciding a broad definitional question unnecessarily, I would vote for Respondent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Given the VPPA’s text and structure, a free, general-interest sports-news website with incidental short clips is not most naturally a “video tape service provider” “engaged in the business … of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials.” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(4). Applying the Court’s pragmatic, context-sensitive approach to statutory scope (cf. Yates v. United States and Fischer v. United States), the better reading is that Congress targeted entities whose business model centrally depends on providing video content, not sites where video is ancillary to news and advertising. Even if there is a circuit split, this case appears vehicle-impaired because independent issues—especially whether the alleged disclosures qualify as “personally identifiable information” and whether the alleged harm is concrete under Spokeo and TransUnion—could defeat jurisdiction or liability regardless of the provider-definition question. In light of TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021), standing cannot rest on a bare statutory violation divorced from a concrete harm closely related to traditionally recognized privacy injuries, and the uncertainty on PII/traceability counsels against expanding the VPPA’s reach here.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a free sports-news website that posts short video clips qualifies as a “video tape service provider” under the Video Privacy Protection Act (VPPA), such that its alleged disclosure of users’ video-viewing information triggers VPPA liability.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 2710 (the Video Privacy Protection Act), including the definitions in § 2710(a) and the disclosure prohibition in § 2710(b)(1).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Salazar argues that the Sixth Circuit adopted an unduly narrow interpretation of the VPPA that fails to account for modern internet video delivery, and that websites like 247Sports fall within the statute’s coverage even if they provide video clips for free rather than renting or selling tapes; he urges Supreme Court review to resolve a circuit split over the proper interpretation of the VPPA’s coverage (including who counts as a covered video provider and/or who counts as a protected consumer) and contends this case is a clean vehicle because it comes after final judgment with no ongoing proceedings below.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Paramount/247Sports argues certiorari should be denied because (1) the VPPA was aimed at businesses like video rental/sales/subscription services and does not extend to a free sports news site offering incidental clips; (2) Salazar’s complaint fails for multiple independent reasons regardless of how the Court answers the “consumer”/coverage question, making the case a poor vehicle; (3) the issues should continue to percolate, and other pending petitions/cases (e.g., NBA-related litigation and Solomon) raise related but distinct splits and posture concerns (including interlocutory/final-judgment problems and separate disputes over what counts as “personally identifiable information”).

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s functional-equivalence argument most directly presses on my concern about freezing the VPPA in 1988, but it still asks us to untether “similar audio visual materials” and “delivery” from the statute’s commercial video-distribution frame—“engaged in the business” and the linked “consumer” definition (“renter, purchaser, or subscriber”)—in a way that risks converting the Act into a broad internet-tracking regime without a clear textual hook. Justice Kagan’s point about the interlocking definitions reinforces that this is not merely a technology-update question; it is a threshold coverage question about whether this respondent is in the business of furnishing video as a product or service. The contextual approach reflected in Yates, and Justice Alito’s caution (invoking Fischer) about expansive readings in a statutory-damages scheme, strengthens my institutional view that any major extension to ad-supported news sites should come from Congress. I would therefore affirm on the narrow ground that this respondent is not a “video tape service provider” on these facts, leaving PII and other vehicle complications aside.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s functional-equivalence point—that categorical exclusion of internet video would frustrate the VPPA’s privacy purpose—does not overcome the enacted limits: a covered entity must be “engaged in the business” of “rental, sale, or delivery” of “prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials,” language anchored to a particular kind of video-distribution enterprise rather than any website transmitting clips. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, the statute’s linked “consumer” definition (“renter, purchaser, or subscriber”) confirms that Congress regulated a commercial provider–customer relationship, and Sotomayor’s approach risks collapsing that narrowing structure into a general internet-tracking regime. The contextual method reflected in Yates (invoked by Roberts/Kagan) properly cabins “similar audio visual materials” by its 1988 neighbors, and Fischer-style caution (noted by Justice Alito) counsels against extending a statutory-damages scheme absent a clear textual hook. Eichenberger and similar cases do not move the needle here because they address PII/subscriber questions once the defendant is already plausibly in the covered line of business; they do not justify expanding § 2710(a)(4) beyond its original public meaning.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s functional-equivalence argument is the strongest point for petitioner, but it still asks us to treat “similar audio visual materials” and “delivery” as essentially free-floating terms untethered from the statute’s video-store paradigm and its narrowing requirement that the entity be “engaged in the business” of rental, sale, or delivery. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, the VPPA’s interlocking definitions—especially “consumer” as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber”—presuppose a commercial video-distribution relationship, and extending the Act to an ad-supported news site with incidental clips would strain that structure and create sweeping damages exposure without clear textual notice. The contextual approach reflected in Yates, and the institutional caution against atextual breadth in Fischer (noted by the Chief), reinforce reading the general phrase “similar audio visual materials” in light of its specific neighbors rather than converting the VPPA into a general internet-tracking statute. Eichenberger and similar lower-court cases may illuminate “subscriber” or standing once an entity is plausibly a covered provider, but they do not answer the threshold coverage question under § 2710(a)(4) here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point seriously: the VPPA’s linked definitions and the phrase “engaged in the business” must do limiting work, and we should avoid an interpretation that would sweep in every ad-supported publisher with an embedded clip. But their parade-of-horribles depends on treating my reading as boundless; courts can and do draw administrable, context-sensitive lines that distinguish incidental video from systematic video “delivery” as part of a business model, consistent with the statute’s privacy-protective purpose. Yates, as Justice Kagan invokes it, supports narrowing a general term when breadth would become atextual and incoherent; it does not require us to confine “delivery” and “similar audio visual materials” to obsolete distribution formats when the same identity-to-viewing-choice harm now occurs through online delivery at scale. Fischer’s caution (raised by Justice Alito) reinforces careful limiting principles in a damages regime, but it does not justify categorically excluding internet video providers from coverage where the text can reasonably accommodate them, leaving PII/consumer/vehicle issues for remand.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is the anti-obsolescence one: “delivery” and “similar audio visual materials” should be read to reach modern modes of transmitting video where the same privacy harm occurs. But the text’s architecture still matters—§ 2710(a)(4)’s provider definition is tethered to being “engaged in the business” of “rental, sale, or delivery” of the specified materials, and the “consumer” definition (renter/purchaser/subscriber) presupposes a commercial video-service relationship; as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, treating an ad-supported news site with incidental clips as such a business makes the limiting words do no work and yields an unadministrably sweeping damages regime. Yates (and Justice Alito’s Fischer point) reinforces that we should read general terms like “similar audio visual materials” in light of their neighbors rather than extracting them to create an internet-tracking statute by implication. Sotomayor’s proposed functional line-drawing is not implausible in the abstract, but here it lacks a clear textual stopping point that preserves the statute’s linked definitions, so I would affirm on the narrow ground that respondent is not a covered “video tape service provider” on these facts.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s functional-equivalence argument rightly highlights that the privacy harm the VPPA targets can occur online, but under a textualist approach that purpose cannot displace the statute’s narrowing words—“engaged in the business” of “rental, sale, or delivery” of “prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, reading “delivery” and “similar” untethered from their neighbors (and from the linked “consumer” definition of “renter, purchaser, or subscriber”) risks converting a video-store paradigm into a general internet-tracking regime with sweeping statutory damages and little notice. Yates supports that context-sensitive reading: general terms take meaning from the specific company they keep, so “similar” cannot be made boundless to cover any site that transmits video. Eichenberger and related cases do not move me because, as Justice Alito notes, they address standing/subscriber issues once coverage is established, not the threshold question whether this respondent is a covered “video tape service provider” at all.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that the VPPA’s core privacy harm—linking identity to viewing choices—can occur through online video delivery, and her functional approach is the strongest argument against freezing the statute in 1988. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the Act’s interlocking definitions—“engaged in the business” of “rental, sale, or delivery” of tapes or “similar audio visual materials,” and “consumer” as a “renter, purchaser, or subscriber”—presuppose a commercial video-distribution relationship that a free news site with incidental clips does not fit. Yates’s context-sensitive method supports reading “similar” and “delivery” in light of their statutory neighbors, and (as Justice Alito notes with Fischer) the combination of a damages regime and an atextually broad construction raises serious notice and administrability concerns.
